2.text: this peculiar vamp, the Chukchee winter boot has a square-shaped toe. The

3.text: same shape is used for the summer boots of seal-skin or curried leather, though

4.text: the vamp in the latter consists of a plain piece sewed to the sole. Other

5.text: tribes of northeastern Asia neighboring on the Chukchee generally wear boots

6.text: with pointed toes. In the Yakut boots the toes even bend upward with a

7.text: long curved strip, somewhat resembling the well-known mediæval form. The

8.text: natives are well aware of the peculiar square shape of the toe of the Chuk-

9.text: chee boot. In one of the legends of the local Russians about their early war

10.text: with the Chukchee, a party of the latter is discovered by means of the square-

11.text: shaped grass insoles which they had thrown into the river flowing past their

12.text: camp. The soles for the coldest time of the year are made of patches of

13.text: very tough skin taken from between the four toes of the reindeer’s foot.

14.text: These patches are covered with thick tufts of hair, dirty white in color, and

15.text: almost as stiff as bristles. They are sewed together, fashioned into a sole,

16.text: and then well dried. The sole has the hair side out, so that the whole covering

17.text: of the man, from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot, literally bristles

18.text: with hair, like the skin of an animal.

19.text: In former times the Maritime Chukchee on the Arctic shores used the

20.text: leg-skins of the white bear for making winter boots, including the soles. This

21.text: fact was also noted by Nordenskiöld. These parts of the bear-skin are
21.resolved: ö = o + U+0308 (diaeresis), in the proper name Nordenskiöld — English prose, ordinary orthography, not Tier-1 notation.

22.text: exceedingly tough and covered with thick white hair, so they serve the pur-

23.text: pose well. Nowadays, however, the skin of a polar bear brings a very good

24.text: price either from Russian or American buyers, so the natives have ceased to

25.text: use it for shoes. Only the elbow-protectors, that form part of the seal-hunter’s

26.text: dress,¹ continue to be made of polar-bear skin. For all other seasons, covering

27.text: about nine months of the year, the soles of boots are made of thong-seal hide

28.text: with the hair side in, or of split walrus-skin. The latter is not so durable as

29.text: ground-seal skin. Notwithstanding the extreme toughness of these hides, the

30.text: herdsmen wear them out quickly, especially in summer. The inland camps

31.text: are always in want of hides for making soles. In the Kolyma country thong-

32.text: seal hides sell for twenty fawn-skins apiece. Even cow’s hide, furnished by

33.text: Yakut traders, is gladly bought at the rate of three reindeer-bucks for one

34.text: hide. Poor people, unable to procure enough hide for soles, make them of

35.text: pieces of skin taken from the neck of old reindeer-bucks. This leather is

36.text: tough enough for soles, especially when taken from wild animals, but it is

37.text: more susceptible to damage by dampness.

38.text: The boot-string is made of strips of curried leather, which are sewed to

39.text: the boot on both sides, a little behind the ankle (Fig. 171, b), and taper
